Course · Whole course on one page

Neural networks in t27: from one neuron to a transformer block

The agents of this project think with neural networks, and here their parts are written as t27 specs with tests, specs the compiler checks. Every widget runs the fn bodies of a specs/ml spec compiled to WebAssembly: move a slider and the spec answers.

Course 10, 27 lessons, a live widget and a t27 spec each: activations, softmax and embeddings, pooling and batch norm, losses, SGD, RMSProp and Adam, backpropagation and XOR, recurrent cells, attention, a transformer block and PPO. Every number is computed by a compiled spec.

Every course is free, for everyone: no sign-up, no email, nothing to pay.

01

Module 1 · One neuron

A neuron sums its inputs and bends the sum: ReLU, the sigmoid and tanh, and where each one stops passing a gradient back.

01

Lesson 1 of 27

ReLU: keep the positive part

You will learnWhat ReLU does to a positive and to a negative input, and why a slope of 0 stops a unit from learning.

A neuron adds up its weighted inputs and passes the sum through an activation. ReLU is the plainest one, max(0, x): a positive sum goes through unchanged and a negative one becomes 0. Its slope is 1 or 0, and a slope of 0 is a unit that has stopped learning, because no gradient flows back through it. A leaky slope fixes that: with a slope of 0.1, x = -2 gives -0.2 and passes back a gradient of 0.1. The spec relu_activation.t27 computes both curves the widget draws.

Try it

Put x at -2 and read the slope with and without the leak; then find the slope at x = 1.5.

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Lesson 2 of 27

The sigmoid: a number into a probability

You will learnHow the sigmoid maps any input to a probability, and why its slope limits deep networks.

The sigmoid 1 / (1 + e^-x) squeezes the whole number line into 0 to 1, which is why it reads as a probability: 2 becomes 0.8808 and -4 becomes 0.018. Its slope is s (1 - s), computed from the output s itself, and it is largest at 0, where it is 0.25; at x = 8 it is 0.000335. A gradient that passes back through a stack of sigmoids is multiplied by at most 0.25 at each one, which is why deep sigmoid networks trained slowly. The spec sigmoid_activation.t27 computes the curve and the slope.

Try it

Find the input where the probability is 0.5; then drag to 6 and read how little slope is left.

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Lesson 3 of 27

tanh and saturation

You will learnWhy tanh is centred on zero, and where its slope falls so low that a unit stops learning.

tanh is a sigmoid stretched to -1..1 and centred on 0, so a layer of tanh units passes on values that average near zero, and its slope reaches 1 at the centre. It still saturates: at 2.5 the output is 0.9866 and the slope only 0.0266. The red band marks every input where the slope is under 0.1, beyond about 1.8 on either side, and a unit whose inputs live there barely learns. The spec tanh_activation.t27 computes the curve, the slope and its own batch, tanh of 0, 1 and 2: 0, 0.762 and 0.964.

Try it

Drag x until the band starts and read the slope there; then compare the slope at 0 and at 2.5.

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Module 2 · New bends

The smooth curves of current models: GELU with its dip, Swish with its knob, and ELU with a floor instead of a cliff.

04

Lesson 4 of 27

GELU: a dip below zero

You will learnWhat GELU computes, why it dips below zero, and how close its tanh shortcut comes.

GELU weighs x by the chance that a standard normal draw is below it: GELU(x) = x Phi(x). A large positive input passes, a large negative one vanishes, and in between the curve dips to about -0.17 near x = -0.75 before it rises. BERT and GPT use it in their feed-forward layers. The exact form needs erf, which the spec computes with the Abramowitz-Stegun fit, good to 1.5e-7, and it also computes the tanh shortcut: at -0.75 they give -0.16997 and -0.17004. The spec gelu_activation.t27 computes both curves and their slopes.

Try it

Find the lowest point of the curve by its slope; then compare the exact and the tanh form at -3.

Open the interactive lesson →
05

Lesson 5 of 27

Swish and SiLU

You will learnHow x times sigmoid(beta x) gates itself, and how one parameter moves it from a smooth curve to ReLU.

Swish is x times sigmoid(beta x), a unit that gates itself. At beta 1 it is called SiLU, and its lowest point is -0.2785 near x = -1.28. Raise beta and the gate sharpens: at beta 8 the curve is ReLU with rounded corners; at beta 0.5 it is a gentle slope through zero. One parameter moves the unit between a smooth curve and a switch, and a network can learn it. The spec silu_swish_activation.t27 computes the curve and its slope for any beta, and its own batch at -2, 0 and 2: -0.238, 0 and 1.762.

Try it

Hold x at -1.28 and raise beta from 1 to 8; then find the beta at which the dip is gone at this scale.

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Lesson 6 of 27

ELU: a floor, not a cliff

You will learnHow ELU keeps a soft negative side with a floor at -alpha, and why its slope never quite dies.

ELU keeps the positive side of ReLU and replaces the cliff on the negative side with alpha (e^x - 1), a curve that flattens toward -alpha. With alpha 1, x = -3 gives -0.9502, already near the floor of -1, and the slope there is 0.0498: small, but not 0, so the unit can still move. Because the negative outputs are not thrown away, a layer's outputs average closer to 0. The spec elu_activation.t27 computes the curve, the slope and the floor, and its own batch at -1, 0 and 2: -0.632, 0 and 2.

Try it

Set alpha to 0.5 and read the floor; then find how far left x must go before the slope is under 0.01.

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Module 3 · A layer

What sits around the neurons: softmax turns scores into a choice, an embedding turns a word into numbers, dropout switches units off.

07

Lesson 7 of 27

Softmax and temperature

You will learnHow softmax turns scores into probabilities that sum to one, and what the temperature does to them.

A classifier ends with one score per class, and softmax turns the scores into probabilities: exp of each score over the sum of all of them. Scores 1, 2 and 3 become 0.090, 0.245 and 0.665. Dividing the scores by a temperature first changes how sure it is: at 0.5 the top score takes 0.867, at 5 the three are 0.27, 0.33 and 0.40. A language model picks its next token from exactly this, and the temperature setting of a chat model is this T. The spec softmax.t27 subtracts the largest score first, so exp never overflows.

Try it

Cool the temperature to 0.1 and read the three probabilities; then make a tie and heat it.

Open the interactive lesson →
08

Lesson 8 of 27

Embeddings

You will learnHow a token becomes a row of numbers, and why learning changes only the rows that were read.

A network cannot multiply a word, so each token is an index into a table with one row of numbers per token, and looking a token up copies its row. In the spec the table has 4 tokens of width 2 and row v holds (10 v, 10 v + 1), so token 2 reads (20, 21). Learning sends the gradient back only to the rows that were read, and a token read twice collects both: gradient rows (1, 2) and (3, 4) on token 2 add up to (4, 6). The spec embedding_layer.t27 computes the lookup and the gradient.

Try it

Read token 2 twice and then tokens 1 and 3; count the rows whose gradient is not 0 each time.

Open the interactive lesson →
09

Lesson 9 of 27

Dropout

You will learnWhy switching units off while training helps, and why the survivors must be scaled.

While training, dropout switches off a share p of the units at random, so the rest cannot lean on any one of them. The units that survive must then be scaled, or the next layer would see the signal at another size in training than at inference. Inverted dropout scales them by 1 / (1 - p) while training: with p = 0.5, input 1, 2, 3, 4 becomes 2, 0, 6, 0, and inference is a plain pass. Classic dropout keeps 1, 0, 3, 0 and scales by 0.5 at inference instead. The spec dropout_layer.t27 uses a fixed mask, keep, drop, keep, drop, so the numbers are the same every time.

Try it

Compare the outputs of the four modes; then read the gradient of a dropped unit in training.

Open the interactive lesson →
04

Module 4 · Pictures

Reading a picture in patches: a window averaged over its patch, max pooling, and batch normalisation of features on different scales.

10

Lesson 10 of 27

Patches of a picture

You will learnWhy networks read a picture in patches, and what a 2 x 2 window averaged over each patch gives.

A picture is a grid of numbers, and networks read it in small patches so that the same detector works anywhere in it. Here a 2 x 2 window steps by 2 over a 4 x 4 image whose cell i holds i, and each output is the average of its patch: 2.5, 4.5, 10.5 and 12.5. In the backward pass each output's gradient is split equally over its 4 cells. This is average pooling: a convolution would weight the 4 cells with a learned kernel, and its spec, t27#10612, is not merged yet. The spec avgpool2d_layer.t27 computes both passes.

Try it

Tap each patch and check its average by eye; then switch to the gradient and read what each cell of window 4 receives.

Open the interactive lesson →
11

Lesson 11 of 27

Max pooling

You will learnWhat max pooling keeps, where it remembers taking it from, and where the gradient goes.

Max pooling keeps the largest value of each window and drops the rest, so the network cares less about exactly where a feature sits. On the spec's 4 x 4 grid, 2 x 2 windows with stride 2 keep 4, 8, 9 and -2, taken from cells 5, 6, 13 and 11. Overlapping 3 x 3 windows with stride 1 keep 8, 8, 9 and 9. In the backward pass each window's whole gradient goes to its maximum: gradients 1, 2, 3 and 4 land on cells 5, 6, 13 and 11, and every other cell gets 0. The spec maxpool2d_layer.t27 computes the outputs, their positions and the gradient.

Try it

Switch to 3 x 3 windows and find the cell two outputs share; then turn on the gradient for 2 x 2 windows.

Open the interactive lesson →
12

Lesson 12 of 27

Batch normalisation

You will learnHow batch norm puts features on different scales on one scale, and what it uses at inference.

Features on different scales pull a network around: in the spec's batch one feature is ten times another. Batch normalisation subtracts each feature's batch mean and divides by its spread, so the features 1, 2, 3, 4 and 10, 20, 30, 40 both come out as -1.34, -0.45, 0.45 and 1.34, and -1, -1, 1, 1 comes out as -1 and 1. A learned gamma and beta then scale and shift it back where that helps. At inference the layer uses running averages instead of the batch: with mean 0, variance 1, gamma 1 and beta 0.25, the inputs 1, 2 and 3 give 1.25, 2.25 and 3.25. The spec batchnorm_layer.t27 computes both.

Try it

Compare the two normalised columns; then set the running mean 2 and variance 4 and read the inference outputs.

Open the interactive lesson →
05

Module 5 · The error

How wrong a guess is, as one number: mean squared error, cross-entropy for probabilities, and the Huber loss for outliers.

13

Lesson 13 of 27

Mean squared error

You will learnHow MSE turns every miss into one number, why it chases large errors, and where its gradient points.

A loss turns all the misses of a model into one number to push down. Mean squared error averages the squared misses: predictions 1.5, 2 and 2 against targets 1, 2 and 3 cost (0.25 + 0 + 1) / 3 = 0.4167. Squaring makes a miss of 2 cost 4 times a miss of 1, so MSE chases large errors. Its gradient for each prediction is 2 (p - t) / n, here 0.333, 0 and -0.667: each prediction is pushed back toward its target. As a function of one prediction the loss is a parabola, a bowl with one bottom. The spec mse_loss.t27 computes the loss and the gradient.

Try it

Move prediction 2 onto its target and read the loss; then drag along the bowl and find its bottom.

Open the interactive lesson →
14

Lesson 14 of 27

Cross-entropy

You will learnWhy cross-entropy charges a confident wrong answer so much, and why that is what trains a classifier.

A classifier outputs a probability, and cross-entropy charges -log of the probability it gave to the true answer. Predictions 0.8, 0.3 and 0.9 against answers 1, 0 and 1 cost 0.2284 on average. Being sure and right is nearly free: 0.99, 0.01 and 0.99 cost 0.0101. Being sure and wrong is expensive: 0.01, 0.99 and 0.01 cost 4.6052, and toward 0 the cost grows without bound, which is why the spec clips p to [1e-7, 1 - 1e-7]. Its gradient is largest exactly where the model is sure and wrong. The spec binary_crossentropy_loss.t27 computes the loss and the gradient, from probabilities or from logits.

Try it

Drag prediction 0 toward 0.01 and watch the curve; then read the gradient bars at 0.5, 0.5 and 0.5.

Open the interactive lesson →
15

Lesson 15 of 27

The Huber loss

You will learnHow the Huber loss treats a small error like squared error and a large one linearly, so outliers pull less.

Squared error lets one outlier dominate: an error of 3 costs 4.5 as half its square, as much as 36 errors of 0.5. Huber is half the square while |e| is within delta and then grows only linearly, delta |e| - delta^2 / 2, so with delta 1 that error costs 2.5. The two pieces meet with the same value and slope, and the gradient never grows past delta: a far-off point pulls on the model with a bounded force. For the spec's pair of errors 0.5 and 3 the mean is 1.3125, against 2.3125 for half the square. The spec huber_loss.t27 computes both.

Try it

Set delta to 0.5 and drag the error to 3; then find where the two curves part.

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Module 6 · Downhill

Walking down the loss: gradient descent with momentum, RMSProp that ignores the gradient's size, and Adam that combines them.

16

Lesson 16 of 27

Gradient descent

You will learnHow gradient descent walks down a loss, what momentum adds, and why too large a rate never settles.

Training is walking downhill on the loss. Gradient descent moves a weight by -lr times its gradient each step; in the spec the loss is (x - 3)^2 from x = 0, and lr 0.1 reaches 2.99996 in 50 steps. Momentum adds a share of the last move, which speeds up a long slope and overshoots a sharp bottom: at 0.9 the weight shoots past 3 to about 5.13 and rings down to 3.09 after 50 steps. Nesterov takes the gradient one step ahead and swings less, to about 4.25. Too large a rate never settles: at lr 1 the weight bounces between 0 and 6 for good. The spec sgd.t27 computes every step.

Try it

Find the largest learning rate that still settles without momentum; then add momentum 0.9 and count the swings.

Open the interactive lesson →
17

Lesson 17 of 27

RMSProp

You will learnHow RMSProp divides each step by a running root mean square, so the step no longer depends on the gradient's size.

The right step size depends on the size of the gradient, and different weights see gradients a million times apart. RMSProp keeps a running mean of the squared gradient, the cache, and divides each step by its root, so the step has no units: with a constant gradient of 0.001, 0.5 or 1000 the weight moves by exactly the same 0.0316 on step 1 and walks the same path, reaching -0.0914 after 100 steps at lr 0.01. The decay sets how slowly the cache fills: at 0.99 the same 100 steps end at -1.0261. The spec rmsprop.t27 computes the weight and the cache.

Try it

Switch between the three gradients and check that the lines do not move; then raise the decay to 0.99.

Open the interactive lesson →
18

Lesson 18 of 27

Adam

You will learnHow Adam combines momentum with a running scale, and why its bias correction makes step 1 a fixed size.

Adam combines the two ideas: m, a running mean of the gradient, as in momentum, and v, a running mean of its square, as in RMSProp; the step is lr m / sqrt(v). Both start at 0 and are too small early on, so Adam divides them by 1 - beta^t, and on step 1 that makes the move exactly lr times the sign of the gradient: gradients 2, -40 and 0.5 all move their weights by 0.001. On the spec's bowl (x - 3)^2 at lr 0.1, Adam rises from 0, overshoots to about 3.18 and settles at 3.00005 by step 200. The spec adam.t27 computes every step.

Try it

Give the three gradients very different sizes and read the weights after step 1; then find where the path tops out.

Open the interactive lesson →
07

Module 7 · Learning

Where the gradients come from and what they achieve: backpropagation through a layer, a network that learns XOR, and LAMB for large batches.

19

Lesson 19 of 27

Backpropagation

You will learnHow the gradient of each weight and each input of a layer follows from the gradient of its outputs.

To learn, every weight needs to know how the loss changes when it moves. Backpropagation answers one layer at a time: given g, how much the loss wants each output to move, the weight from input i to output o gets g_o x_i, and input i gets the sum over o of W[o][i] g_o, which it hands on to the layer below. With inputs (1, 2, 3) and g = (1, 0.5) the weight gradients are 1, 2, 3 and 0.5, 1, 1.5, and the input gradients 0.5, 2 and 3.5. The layer is linear, so moving x0 by 1 moves the loss g . y from 15.25 to 15.75, by its gradient 0.5. The spec dense_layer.t27 computes all three.

Try it

Set g = (1, 0) and read which edges go dark; then set g = (-2, 1) and check the input gradients by hand.

Open the interactive lesson →
20

Lesson 20 of 27

Learning XOR

You will learnWhy one neuron cannot learn XOR, and how a hidden layer trained by backpropagation does.

XOR is 1 when exactly one of two inputs is 1. No straight line separates the cases that give 1 from those that give 0, so a single neuron cannot learn it. A hidden layer bends the space: the spec trains a 2-8-1 network of ReLUs by backpropagation, lr 0.05, from fixed initial weights. Its loss falls from 0.8896 in epoch 1 to 1.8e-13 after 2000 epochs, and its four answers come out within 4e-7 of 0, 1, 1 and 0. The widget runs that training in your browser, from scratch for every point of the curve. The spec mlp.t27 holds the network and the test that it learns.

Try it

Drag the epochs back to 100 and read the four answers; then find the epoch where the curve stops falling.

Open the interactive lesson →
21

Lesson 21 of 27

LAMB and large batches

You will learnHow LAMB scales each layer's step by its own weight norm, so one learning rate suits layers of every size.

Training with very large batches needs a large learning rate, and one rate can be too large for a small layer and too small for a big one. LAMB takes an Adam-style update for each layer and rescales it by the trust ratio, the layer's weight norm, capped at 10, over the update's norm, so every layer moves by the same fraction of itself. In the spec, the weights (1, 2) times a scale take a step whose norm is 0.001 times theirs: 0.00447 at scale 2, and once the weight norm passes 10, near scale 4.47, the step stays at 0.01. The spec lamb.t27 computes the update for one layer and for two at once.

Try it

Read the step at scales 1 and 2 and compare; then drag past the bend and explain why the line goes flat.

08

Module 8 · Memory and attention

Networks that read a sequence: a recurrent cell and its fading echo, the gates of an LSTM, and attention over every position at once.

22

Lesson 22 of 27

A recurrent cell

You will learnHow a recurrent cell carries a state from step to step, and why that memory fades.

A sentence comes one word at a time, and a recurrent cell carries a state h from one step to the next: h' = tanh(W_x x + W_h h + b). In the spec's tiny cell W_x is 1 and W_h 0.5, so a single pulse gives 0.7616, 0.3634 and 0.1797: the memory of it roughly halves each step. A second pulse at step 3 lifts h to 0.7968, a little above where the single pulse began, because the old memory is still there. After 8 steps only 0.0466 is left. That fading is why plain cells forget long contexts. The spec rnn_cell.t27 computes each step.

Try it

Load one pulse and read how many steps it takes to fall under 0.1; then make the input alternate.

Open the interactive lesson →
23

Lesson 23 of 27

LSTM gates

You will learnHow the forget, input and output gates of an LSTM decide what the cell keeps, writes and shows.

An LSTM cell keeps a separate memory c and three gates, each a sigmoid between 0 and 1: forget scales the old memory, input lets in new content g, and output decides how much of the memory to show. c' = f c + i g and h' = o tanh(c'). In the spec's fixture every weight is 0, so each gate is the sigmoid of its bias: with the forget gate at 0.9975 and the input gate at 0.0025, a memory of 1 comes out as 0.9975, and the output is 0.7587. Because c passes through with only a multiply by f, its gradient survives many steps too. The spec lstm_single.t27 computes the cell.

Try it

Load Remember and then Forget and compare the new memory; then write with the input gate open.

Open the interactive lesson →
24

Lesson 24 of 27

Attention

You will learnHow attention scores every query against every key, what a softmax over each row gives, and what the causal mask removes.

Attention lets each position decide which other positions to read. Every query is scored against every key, q . k / sqrt(d), and a softmax turns each row of scores into weights that sum to 1; the output is the values averaged by those weights. Two heads do it on the two halves of the vector. With a causal mask a position cannot read the future: in head 0, position 0 reads only itself, position 1 splits 0.452 and 0.548, and position 2 spreads 0.230, 0.321 and 0.449. Without the mask every row spreads over all three keys, from 0.21 to 0.47. The spec attention_mechanism.t27 computes every weight on its own fixture.

Try it

Turn the mask off and on and read row 0; then compare the two heads on row 2.

Open the interactive lesson →
09

Module 9 · The transformer and the reward

The parts of a transformer and of an agent: positions as clocks, one encoder block, and PPO, which learns from reward without lurching.

25

Lesson 25 of 27

Positional encoding

You will learnHow sines and cosines at falling frequencies give every position its own vector, and why a shift is a turn.

Attention treats its input as a set, so the order of the words has to be added to them. The sinusoidal encoding gives each position d numbers: the sin and cos of the position times a frequency that falls by 10000^(2/d) from pair to pair. With d = 8 the four pairs turn by 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 radians per position, like the hands of four clocks: position 5 reads -0.959, 0.284 in its fast pair and 0.005, 1.000 in its slow one. Each pair has length 1, and a shift by k positions turns every pair by its own fixed angle. The spec positional_encoding.t27 computes every value.

Try it

Step from position 0 to 1 and watch which clock moves; then jump to 37 and find the pair that still points up.

Open the interactive lesson →
26

Lesson 26 of 27

An encoder block

You will learnWhat one transformer encoder block does to its input, and what moving the norms in front changes.

A transformer layer is two sublayers, each wrapped in a residual add and a layer norm: self-attention mixes the positions, then a feed-forward net of width 8 works on each position alone. In the post-norm order of the original paper the block ends with a norm, so every output row has mean 0 and variance 1.000. Pre-norm puts the norms in front of each sublayer and ends on a residual add, so its rows come out at variances 2.73, 3.33 and 0.96; deep stacks train more easily that way, with one norm added at the very top. The spec encoder_block.t27 runs one block on 3 positions, d_model 4 and 2 heads.

Try it

Switch between post-norm and pre-norm and read the row variances; then find the position head 1 reads most.

Open the interactive lesson →
27

Lesson 27 of 27

PPO and the reward

You will learnHow PPO turns a reward into a policy update, and how its clip keeps one update from going too far.

An agent learns from reward by making good actions more likely. PPO measures a change of policy by the ratio r of the new probability of an action to the old one and multiplies it by the advantage A, how much better the action did than expected. Then it clips: once r has moved more than eps the way A rewards, the objective goes flat. At r = 1.5, A = 1 and eps 0.2 the raw r A is 1.5, but PPO counts 1.2, so one batch cannot push the policy far. On the spec's batch, ratios 1, 1.1 and 0.9 with advantages 2, 1.5 and 3, the policy loss is -2.1167. The spec ppo_clip_loss.t27 computes it.

Try it

Make the advantage negative and find where the curve goes flat now; then widen eps to 0.5.

TRI CLAW

The agent behind t27, in Telegram and on GitHub

TRI CLAW is the project's agent: it writes and checks .t27 specs with you. Three ways to use it.

  • Free, with your own key

    Add your own API key (NVIDIA or z.ai today) and the agent runs on it. Add more keys any time.

    Add a key in Telegram ↗

  • We do it for you

    No keys to keep: join the club in our Telegram bot and the agent runs on ours. The bot shows the price before you pay.

    Join the club in Telegram ↗

  • On GitHub

    TRI CLAW is also a GitHub App, built to check the .t27 specs a pull request changes. It is not open to other repositories yet.
